Channels: Chat, Telegram & Email ​

A channel is a surface onto the same PRIME, the same runs, and the same memory. The dashboard is one; Telegram is another; transactional email is a one-way third. Nothing about the orchestrator changes per channel — an adapter owns only its wire protocol, and the shared chat engine owns the turn loop, the toolbelt, approvals, and the activity log.

For Telegram setup steps, see Connecting Telegram. This page is about how the machinery underneath works.

The adapter contract ​

Every messaging channel implements a deliberately small interface:

ts
interface ChannelAdapter {
  readonly id: ChannelId;          // 'telegram' | 'discord' | 'whatsapp' | 'imessage'
  init(deps: ChannelDeps): void | Promise<void>;
  stop(): void;
}

Adapters register themselves at module load; startChannels() starts whatever is registered and never lets one adapter's failure stop the others, and stopChannels() tears them all down on shutdown. Only Telegram is implemented today — the other three ids exist as the stable keys for config and identity rows.

startChannels() is called only when the process is not in cloud mode. Channels run as the single fixed local tenant, which is why the sections below describe a flat allow-list rather than per-member identity.

Per-org channel config ​

Channel configuration lives in one store shared by all channels, keyed by (orgId, channel):

FieldPurpose
enabledWhether the adapter should connect
secretsChannel-specific credentials, e.g. { botToken }
publicCfgNon-secret settings, e.g. { allowedUserIds }
webhookSecretMinted on first save; identifies the org for an inbound webhook path

Secrets are envelope-encrypted at rest whenever a master key is configured, and the UI view never receives a raw secret — only a set flag and a last-3 hint. Telegram additionally migrates the legacy memory/telegram.json (itself seeded once from TELEGRAM_* environment variables) into this store on first read, so an existing install keeps its token with no interruption. See Settings for where each of these is configured.

Inbound: message → turn ​

A chat message becomes one of two things, decided by whether the chat is focused on a run:

Focused means the chat has bound itself to one run (/focus, /newrun, or the Focus button). Non-command text and media then go into that run, and the reply comes back through the run-event relay rather than as a chat turn. Focus is cleared automatically if the run is gone or cancelled.

Main-chat turns go through the durable chat engine. One worker exists per (org, conversation), so turns in the same chat serialize across browser tabs and Telegram while different chats drain in parallel. An accepted turn is written onto the ChatConversation record before it is acknowledged, so it survives a restart:

PendingChatTurn fieldPurpose
id, text, attachmentsThe queued message
sourcedashboard | telegram
channelChatIdTelegram destination, so the renderer can be reattached after a restart
userIdActing member (cloud); absent for the local/system tenant
statequeued | running

At most 10 turns may wait; an eleventh is refused with a queue-full message rather than dropped. On boot, resumePendingChatTurns() requeues them — the dashboard's are recovered during server boot, Telegram's wait until the bot has reconnected so their replies have somewhere to go.

Attachments are handed to PRIME as absolute paths, not as inline content: files for the main chat land in the chat-uploads dir, files for a focused run land in that run's assets dir prefixed up- so the asset sweep skips them.

Outbound: the ChannelUi ​

An adapter implements one callback interface and gets a native rendering of a turn:

CallbackFires when
onTurnStartThe message left the FIFO and its turn is running
onDeltaPRIME streamed a chunk of reply text
onToolStatusPRIME called a tool, or a delegated agent reported progress
onWorkingHeartbeat (every 3s) while blocked on a long tool call
onQueuedThe message was queued behind an in-flight turn
onConfirm / onConfirmResolvedAn approval card is raised, then settled
onError, onTurnEndFailure, and completion (including cancellation)

The deliverFile hook is what backs the send_file brain tool. It is optional: on the dashboard there is no chat to deliver into, so the tool reports that it only works in a chat channel rather than silently failing.

Telegram: connection ​

The adapter long-polls; there is no webhook. On connect it calls getMe to validate the token, calls deleteWebhook (a stale webhook makes getUpdates return 409), registers the slash-command list, then loops getUpdates with a 50-second timeout and allowed_updates: ['message', 'callback_query'].

The service can be reconfigured live from Settings with no restart:

  • token or enabled changed → tear down the loop and start a fresh one;
  • only the allowed-ids changed → mutate the live allow-set in place.

Applies are serialized, so rapid saves cannot interleave a stop with a start. Poll failures back off exponentially from 1s to a 30s ceiling. A 409 is surfaced verbatim in the connection status — one process at a time may poll a given bot token, so that error usually means a second instance is running. A 401 is reported as an invalid token. See Troubleshooting for the operational side.

Allowed senders ​

Authorization is a flat allow-list of Telegram user ids held as a mutable Set:

  • only private chats are handled — group, supergroup, and channel updates are dropped, as are messages from other bots;
  • every sender is recorded (so Settings can list who has messaged the bot) before the authorization check;
  • an unauthorized sender gets exactly one reply, containing their own user id and instructions to authorize it from Settings; subsequent messages are silent, so an unknown sender cannot be used to generate traffic;
  • unauthorized callback-button presses are answered with "Not authorized."

Because the allow-list is global rather than per-member, every allow-listed account is the same local superadmin user. Run notices are broadcast to all of them. That is a known limitation of running channels local-only — see Orgs, Auth & Permissions.

Commands and the runs UI ​

Commands are global: they work the same whether or not the chat is focused on a run.

GroupCommands
Main chat/clear, /new, /cancel, /status, /help, /id
Runs/runs, /run [id], /newrun <brief>, /focus <id>, /main
Approvals/approve [note], /deny [note]
Files/files [id]
Notifications/mute, /unmute
Discovery/projects, /find <text>

/approve and /deny target the focused run when it is gated, otherwise the first run anywhere with a pending approval.

Beyond commands, runs are driven by inline keyboards. Callback data is namespaced — r: for run actions, cf: for approval cards, stop: for cancelling a turn — so the button sets never collide. A run card shows status, project and branch, the first eight checklist items, and any approval gate; the run's (potentially long) last result is sent as its own chunked message rather than clipped into the card.

Run notices and relays ​

Two bridges connect the run store's live signals to Telegram:

  • Thread events → the chats currently focused on that run, so PRIME's replies and generated files stream in live. Operator echoes are skipped (they are already in the chat), and tool/result/delegation noise is filtered out.
  • Lifecycle notices → every authorized, unmuted chat, labelled by kind (needs input, paused, done, error, cancelled) with an Open button. A run parked at an approval gate instead renders Approve/Deny buttons for that exact change.

A chat already focused on a run is not interrupted by that run's lifecycle notices — it is watching the thread live — unless the notice is an actionable approval gate, which has no thread event of its own.

Both relays are fail-soft by construction: they run off store observers and must never throw, because a failure there cannot be allowed to break a store write. A "typing…" indicator is kept alive on a 4-second cadence while a focused run is active, since Telegram's typing action expires after about five seconds. See Reflexes & Events for the other consumer of the same notice bus.

Formatting and streaming ​

Telegram cannot stream tokens, so the renderer simulates it: send one message immediately for instant feedback, then edit it as text accrues — throttled to 1.5s — with a live status footer and a ⏹ Stop button, and roll over to a fresh message as the text approaches the length ceiling.

PRIME's markdown is converted to Telegram's narrow HTML subset (<b>, <i>, <s>, <code>, <pre>, <a>, <blockquote>); everything else is flattened to readable text. Headings become bold, bullets become •, horizontal rules become an em-dash run, and markdown tables — which Telegram cannot render — are preserved inside <pre> so their alignment survives. Inline code spans are treated as opaque, so emphasis markers inside them are never mangled. An unfinished code fence mid-stream is auto-closed for that paint and reopened on the next one.

Two fallbacks make this robust rather than brittle: if Telegram rejects the generated HTML with a parse error, the message is re-sent as plain text and that message stays plain; and a "message is not modified" error is treated as success. Rendering never breaks a turn.

Files ​

send_file delivers a file from disk to the current chat. The path is resolved defensively: a bare filename resolves under the chat-uploads dir, anything else must resolve to an existing file under the data root. Telegram then chooses the wire form by extension and size — PNG/JPEG/WebP under the photo ceiling go as photos with an inline preview; SVG and GIF are deliberately excluded (Telegram rejects SVG as a photo, and sending a GIF as a photo would flatten the animation) and ride as documents.

Channel-specific limits ​

LimitValueWhere it bites
Message text4096 charsTelegram's hard ceiling
Chunk split threshold3500 chars of source markdownWide margin, since HTML tags don't count toward the visible limit
Caption1024 charsCaptions, not message text — clipped with an ellipsis
Inbound file download20 MBTelegram's getFile ceiling for bots; larger files are refused with a message
Photo send10 MBAbove this an image goes as a document
Document send50 MBAbove this the send throws
Files per /files10The remainder is reported, not sent
Chat queue10 turnsShared with the dashboard, per conversation
Streaming edit interval1.5sFlood-control margin
Media-group batching800msAlbum messages are collected into one turn

Rate limiting is handled inside the API client: a 429 with a retry-after of 30 seconds or less is waited out once and the call retried, for both JSON and multipart requests.

The mail channel ​

Mail is one-way and transactional — it carries links, not conversation. The driver is selected by SAIDI_MAIL_DRIVER:

DriverBehaviour
console (default)Logs the message and its link; local and dev never send email
resendPosts to the Resend REST API using SAIDI_RESEND_API_KEY

SAIDI_MAIL_FROM sets the sender. An unset API key with the resend driver logs a warning and drops the message rather than throwing. Three messages exist, each sent as both HTML and plain text: verify your email, reset your password, and workspace invite. Every one of them carries a single-use token in the link — the tokens themselves are described in Orgs, Auth & Permissions.
